claims.text: No gluten-free menu or allergen handling is advertised; the kitchen centers on wheat-based pancakes and French-toast-style items, so cross-contamination with wheat should be assumed.

A genuinely plant-based spice curry (soy meat, turmeric rice) is offered, but no information is published on whether it is prepared separately from dairy/egg-containing pancake items in the same kitchen.

A clearly plant-based main — the 'Healthy Spice Curry,' originally sold as 'Vegan Curry,' using only plant-based ingredients with soy meat instead of animal protein — is a reliable option for vegan diners.
A traditional coffee house centered on toast, cake, and homestyle dishes in a single shared kitchen; cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable and no gluten-free handling is documented.
No vegan menu is documented; food items generally rely on dairy, eggs, or animal-based stock, so dedicated vegan preparation is not indicated.
Plain black hand-roasted coffee is available and is the most reliably plant-based item on offer.

name: cervo bianco（チェルボ ビアンコ） (cervo bianco)

claims.text: Pizza is the core product and is made from wheat dough in a shared wood-fired oven; no gluten-free dough or separate prep is documented, so heavy gluten presence and cross-contamination should be assumed.
Cheese is central to most pizzas and the gelato is dairy-based (Uemura farm milk); shared oven and prep surfaces handle cheese and meat, so dairy cross-contact is likely.

name: 茶粥茶論 月日星 (Chagayu Salon Tsukihiboshi)

claims.text: The meal centers on many small vegetable pickles; Japanese pickles are commonly seasoned with soy sauce, which usually contains wheat, and the menu provides no wheat/gluten labeling.

Some Nara-style pickles can be cured with bonito or other fish-derived seasonings, and the accompanying miso soup most likely uses fish dashi, so a strict vegan should confirm which pickles are fish-free and skip the soup.
The format is buffet-style with rice, tea porridge and 20-plus vegetable pickles you serve yourself, so it is easy to build a vegetable-and-rice plate and to see what you are taking.

name: チャイナダイニング飛天 (China Dining Hiten)

claims.text: This is a dim sum and noodle-focused Chinese kitchen where wheat wrappers, dumplings and wheat noodles are central; no gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed.
Many savory dishes are seasoned in the Chinese style with soy sauce; Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat, so soy-sauce-based dishes are not gluten-free.
The vegan dishes (soy-meat, yuba, greens) are prepared in a kitchen that primarily cooks meat and seafood; no separate-equipment or cross-contact policy is documented.

Vegewel lists the restaurant as having both vegan and vegetarian menus and English-speaking staff plus English menus, which helps when discussing dietary needs, but no specific allergy-handling procedure is described.
A clearly labeled dedicated vegan section and a 7-course vegan tasting menu give plant-based diners reliable, pre-vetted choices rather than ad-hoc substitutions.
The vegetable tanmen and the greens/mushroom/vermicelli soup are built on a vegetable consommé rather than fish dashi, making them suitable for vegans.

Gyoza and other dishes are made with wheat wrappers and almost certainly wheat-based soy sauce in a shared single-cook kitchen; no gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contact should be assumed.
As a Chinese restaurant, dishes are seasoned with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Even tofu and vegetable dishes are cooked alongside and in sauces derived from pork, beef and seafood; vegan separation is not offered.
The signature gyoza are made without garlic, which can help diners avoiding garlic specifically (note: this is not related to gluten or vegan needs).
Kitchen routinely fries breaded items (shrimp fry, cutlets) and serves wheat-based hamburg steak, curry roux and cakes, so heavy gluten cross-contact should be assumed.
A meat- and dairy-centric Western menu with no vegan items documented; shared cooking surfaces with meat and fried foods should be assumed.
A working wheat-flour bakery; flour is used throughout, making cross-contamination unavoidable for gluten-free diners.
Signature and popular items contain dairy and egg (custard cream pan, curry bread, sandwiches); shared bakery equipment means egg/dairy contact is likely across products.
